headline: Rips fluke stack up as the drum run gives way to summer's slow-bass, hot-bite trade
subhead: Doormats are stacking in the rips on the outgoing, triggerfish are eating on the reef sites, and the bass — well, they went north with everybody else's air conditioner.
body_markdown:
Last week the Bay finally settled into its July groove. We came off a string of southwest sea breeze afternoons — 12 to 18 knots by 2 o'clock most days, glassy at dawn — and that pattern held the water clean on the ocean side even as it churned a little chop into the rips by mid-afternoon. New moon passed us on the 14th, so we're climbing out of neap water now, tides building back toward the first quarter next week. That matters more than people think: neap current in the rips means slower drift speeds, which is exactly why the fluke bite held so steady the last several days — less water moving means your bucktail stays in the strike zone longer instead of getting ripped through it.

This week we're on the building side of the cycle, current picking back up day over day into the 21st. That's going to sharpen up the rip bite — faster water stacks bait harder against the structure at Cape May Point and along the edge of the shipping channel, and it'll turn some of these lazy fluke into aggressive ones. Water's warm everywhere right now, upper 70s in the bay shallows by afternoon, mid-70s out in the rips proper. That's summer pattern water — comfortable for fluke, bluefish, and triggerfish, too warm to hold big resident stripers, which is why I want to be straight with you up front: the striper fishing here in mid-July is slow, and it's supposed to be. Most of what wintered and spring-ran through here has pushed north into cooler water. If you want linesiders right now, you're better off waiting for the fall run than beating up the rips looking for a fish that isn't home.

What is home, and eating, is fluke — and they've been good. The outgoing tide out of the Cape May Rips, working the seam where the reef structure drops off into 35 to 45 feet, has been our best water. Four-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom with just enough lift to feel the head tick sand, has been the moneymaker — I had clients into fluke to 6 pounds Tuesday working that exact drift off the Ice Breakers on the last two hours of the ebb. Don't rush the retrieve. These fish are sluggish in the heat and want it crawled, not popped. If the bucktail bite goes quiet, switch to a fluke rig with live spot or a strip of squid and just let it sit — sometimes in July that's the difference between a short and a keeper.

Hereford Inlet has been the bluefish address. Cocktail blues mixed with some genuine choppers in the 4-to-6-pound class have been blitzing bait right at the mouth on the last of the incoming, right around the jetty rocks on the north side. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks in white — thrown into the boils have been getting hit on nearly every cast when the bait's pushed up tight. That bite's tide-dependent and short — usually a 90-minute window either side of the top of the tide before the blues slide back out with the bait. Worth setting your alarm for, not worth showing up late for.

Weakfish have been a mixed bag, and I'll be honest, that's been the toughest read of the week. We're getting them in Delaware Bay proper, working the channel edges off Fortescue and down toward Egg Island, but it's been a dusk-and-dark game — small chartreuse or pink Bass Assassins on 1/4-ounce jigheads, drifted slow over the mud in 15 to 20 feet right as the sun drops. Some nights it's four or five keeper-class weakies in an hour. Other nights it's nothing and you're left wondering if you fished the wrong fifteen minutes of the tide. My honest read: the population's here, but they're not schooled up tight yet the way they can get in a good August. Patience and a thermometer app checking surface temp before you commit to a spot will save you gas.

As for the drum — that run is closed out for the season. Miah Maull, Brandywine Shoal, the mouth of the Cohansey — that whole May show wrapped up weeks ago, and there's nothing left down there worth specifically targeting drum for. If you're still hearing chatter about black drum in mid-July, somebody's telling old stories. Circle back to Fortescue and the bay flats next April.

The bright surprise this month has been triggerfish out on the reef sites — Cape May Reef and the Wildwood Reef in particular. Small pieces of clam or squid fished on light tackle right on the structure in 40 to 60 feet has been steady action, not a numbers game but a fun one, and it's a nice change of pace bite while you're anchored up waiting on a sea bass or fluke drift to develop.

Looking at this week: building tides through the 21st should sharpen the rip bite for fluke — I'd fish the last three hours of the outgoing at Cape May Point, working the deeper edge where the reef drops to 40 feet, and I'd have a bucktail and a bait rod both rigged so you can switch fast if the current picks up faster than expected. If the southwest wind holds its afternoon pattern, morning trips will stay the most comfortable and most productive — get out early, beat the chop, be off the water before the sea breeze fills in past 15 knots. For weakfish, I'd rather be wrong an hour early than late — fish the last hour of daylight into full dark at Fortescue and don't leave until you've given it a real shot on both sides of the tide change. Bass fishing, I'd sit that one out until the water starts cooling in September. Save your gas and your patience for the fish that are actually here.
